stages.title: Constructing the SRAS curve
stages.sub: Understand why short-run aggregate supply slopes upward and how to draw it.

steps.q: A factory wants to push output well above its normal level this month. Wages are sticky and capital is fixed, so it has to pay overtime rates and squeeze more from old machinery. What happens to the cost of producing each extra unit?
steps.hint: Think about paying overtime and running old machines harder to get more output.

steps.q: If it now costs firms more to produce each extra unit, and firms still want to cover their costs, what must happen to the price they need to charge for that output?
steps.hint: If costs per unit go up, can firms still sell at the old price and make the same margin?

steps.q: Now think about the quantity side. As firms accept these higher costs and charge higher prices, what happens to the total amount of output they are willing to produce?
steps.hint: Firms are only willing to push through the extra costs and overtime if they are actually producing more.

steps.q: Put these together: as the price level rises, firms are willing to produce more real GDP, and as they produce more real GDP, the price level needed to cover costs rises further. If you plotted price level against real GDP, which way would this relationship run?
steps.hint: Higher output goes with higher prices here, not lower prices.

steps.q: So on a diagram with price level on the vertical axis and real GDP on the horizontal axis, what have you just drawn by plotting this rising relationship between price level and output?
steps.right: A curve showing output firms supply at each price level in the short run
